data.name: One Giant Leap
data.detailed_description:
One small step for room, One Giant Leap for room-scale.


In One Giant Leap you are equipped with a pair of booster jets for controllers! Fly across the moon, navigating courses to plant the flag and destroying asteroids with rockets.

Featuring ambient space music by Stellardrone and Eric Matyas, you'll experience a meditative trip akin to a flying lucid dream. Explore the moon to discover secret powerups that alter physics and introduce the concept of a rave on the moon.

For the competitive, you can compare course race times with local players and unlock upgrades to your flying abilities after completing courses in record time.

There are multiple mission types currently available, including:
  • 4 Courses
  • 2 Asteroid Hunts
  • 2 Force Flights
  • Free Flight

One Giant Leap was inspired by games like Battlezone, Freelancer, and Tribes Ascend for their immersive space environments and joy of maneuverability.

The boosting locomotion is now also available for developers to use in their own games, via the Moon Motion Toolkit.

Enjoy your moon landing!

data.short_description: Fly across the moon in VR with a motion-controlled jetpack

reviews.review:
One Giant Leap is a VR experience that takes a straightforward idea and builds nearly everything around the pleasure of movement. Instead of presenting the Moon through a demanding simulation filled with technical procedures, it turns the lunar surface into a playground where propulsion, low gravity, speed, and experimentation become the main attractions. Developed and published by Sylvan Studios LLC, the game feels deliberately focused in scope, putting its unusual locomotion system ahead of narrative complexity or elaborate progression.

Its most distinctive feature is the way players travel. Motion controllers function like boosters attached to each hand, allowing you to propel yourself by positioning and moving your arms. It initially requires some adjustment because controlling momentum in virtual reality is considerably different from ordinary stick-based locomotion. Once the system starts making sense, however, moving efficiently becomes satisfying in its own right. Low lunar gravity allows for enormous jumps, extended flights, sudden changes in direction, and dramatic descents toward the surface. Learning to control these movements provides much of the game's challenge.

Several activities give players reasons to improve those flying skills. Four courses emphasize navigation and speed, encouraging increasingly efficient routes as familiarity with the propulsion mechanics improves. Local timing provides a simple score-chasing incentive, making repeated attempts worthwhile for players who enjoy shaving seconds from their performances. Better results can also contribute toward improvements to flying abilities, giving mastery of the movement system a modest sense of progression.

The experience is not limited entirely to racing. Two Asteroid Hunt missions incorporate rockets and give players targets to destroy, adding some straightforward action to the lunar setting. There are also two Force Flight activities that further experiment with locomotion. None of these modes individually provide enormous depth, but together they demonstrate how the central movement concept can support several different styles of play. The relatively small selection of activities remains one of the game's biggest limitations, especially for anyone expecting a lengthy VR campaign.

Free Flight is arguably where the game's unusual concept can be appreciated without pressure. Players can roam around, practice their movements, search for hidden power-ups, and simply enjoy the sensation of crossing the Moon in low gravity. Some discoveries can modify the physics, creating additional opportunities for experimentation. There is even a lunar rave, which makes it clear that realism is secondary to playful VR entertainment. The ambient soundtrack contributes to the atmosphere, helping the quieter exploration sections feel relaxing rather than completely empty.

Presentation is functional and serves the movement mechanics effectively, although the game does not compete with newer high-budget VR productions in environmental detail or visual sophistication. The naturally barren lunar environment works reasonably well with its minimalist presentation, but extended sessions can reveal a lack of scenery variety. Its appeal comes primarily from scale, motion, and the feeling of inhabiting an open lunar environment rather than from highly detailed textures or cinematic spectacle.

Another important consideration is that this is a VR-only game. SteamVR, tracked motion controllers, and appropriate VR equipment are fundamental to how it works. There is no conventional desktop alternative that reproduces the intended gameplay, since the hand-controlled propulsion mechanic depends heavily on motion input. This naturally makes the game much more specialized than an ordinary PC release, but the VR requirement is justified by a design that genuinely incorporates motion controls rather than treating them as a novelty.

Steam Deck compatibility should therefore be considered unsupported for practical purposes. One Giant Leap is designed specifically around SteamVR and tracked VR controllers, so the Steam Deck by itself cannot provide the required gameplay setup. Even if the software could technically be launched through a more complicated external configuration, this is not a conventional handheld experience and should not be purchased with native Steam Deck play as the expectation.

The main weakness is ultimately its limited amount of structured content. The courses, Asteroid Hunt missions, Force Flight activities, exploration, power-ups, and Free Flight mode create some variety, but the package remains comparatively small. Players interested mainly in completing objectives may work through its attractions relatively quickly. Those who enjoy mastering unconventional locomotion, improving times, experimenting with physics, and freely exploring are more likely to extract additional longevity from what is available.

One Giant Leap works best when approached as an experimental VR playground rather than a full-scale space adventure. Its hand-based booster system gives it a recognizable personality, and learning how to fly smoothly across the lunar landscape can be genuinely entertaining. The modest visuals and limited quantity of activities prevent it from becoming an essential VR experience, but its unusual approach to movement gives it enough character to remain memorable for enthusiasts interested in unconventional virtual-reality mechanics.

Rating: 7/10
